title: Principle and Foundation
hook: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Exercises: Ignatius's guided retreat, four stages called weeks, training the soul the way walking trains the body. Your line was exercises for the soul. Did your quiet day make it onto the calendar? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

Why am I here? A child asks it at bedtime. A teenager, slamming a door. A grown-up, at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the drive home from a job they don't love. It's a question that's easy to leave unanswered while we get on with the dishes. Ignatius doesn't. Before the retreat's first week, before a single meditation on sin or mercy or the life of Christ, he sets one short paragraph at the door. It answers that question in a sentence, and everything after it is built on top. Today's word is the paragraph.
screen: `WHY AM I HERE?` → `ASKED AT BEDTIME AND AT 3 A.M.` → `ONE PARAGRAPH AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Ignatius calls it the Principle and Foundation, and it begins with the human person. In his words, put plainly: we are created to praise, to reverence, and to serve God our Lord, and by doing this to save our souls. Three verbs. Praise is the mouth: noticing and saying that something is good. Reverence is the posture: treating God, and the world God made, with care, not carelessness. Serve is the hands: doing something about it. That's the purpose. Then comes the second move, and it's practical. Everything else on the face of the earth, Ignatius says, is created to help us toward that purpose. So things are tools, not goals. A career, a house, a reputation, even health: each one is good to the degree it helps, and becomes a problem to the degree it gets in the way. Tomorrow we'll stay with what that asks of us. For today, just notice the order. Purpose first, then everything else measured against it. Without the first sentence, the second has nothing to measure by. Ignatius isn't alone in saying it. The book of Ecclesiastes, after a long search through pleasure and work and wisdom, comes to rest here, in the Douay-Rheims: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man." This is all man. The whole of a person, in one line. A foundation is the part of a house nobody admires and everybody stands on. Made for this. Get the bottom right, the paragraph suggests, and the rest of the building can go up.
screen: `CREATED TO PRAISE, REVERENCE, SERVE.` · `MOUTH, POSTURE, HANDS.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS A TOOL.` · `PURPOSE FIRST, THEN THE REST.` · then, large: `FOR THIS IS ALL MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write why you're here. Find a scrap of paper, or the notes on your phone. Settle, and breathe. Then write one sentence that begins: I am here to. Don't polish it. It can borrow Ignatius's three verbs, praise, reverence, serve, or it can be in your own words: to love my kids well, to make things, to tell the truth. Read it back once, slowly. Notice which word in it feels most true. If you pray, you can hold the sentence up to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Principle and Foundation. Ignatius's opening paragraph of the Exercises: we're made to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else is meant to help. Today's word.
Your line: made for this. Keep your sentence somewhere you'll see it, and before one decision today, read it and ask whether this helps. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Retreat directors give the Principle and Foundation to retreatants at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, and Jesuit schools and retreat programs return to it as a short statement of what a human life is for.

fork.setup: you're Ignatius, about to open a month-long retreat. what do you put at the very start?
options: one short paragraph on what a person is made for.
a schedule of the day's prayers.
fork.reveal: before the first week, he sets the Principle and Foundation: we are created to praise, reverence and serve God, and everything else is to help.

trapdoor: what you thought: principle and foundation sounds like a business slogan.
what it means: Ignatius's opening paragraph: we are made to praise, reverence and serve God, and all else is to help.
what a scholar hears: the paragraph has two moves, purpose and then the use of creatures measured against it, and the second move sets up the indifference that follows.

notes: Principle and Foundation paraphrased ('put plainly'); no quotation marks. The Mullan (1914) translation is pre-1929 but not on the validator's list.
The 'mouth, posture, hands' reading of praise, reverence, serve is an interpretive gloss, not Ignatius's own; confirm it is fair.
Indifference (the next part of no. 23) is only pointed to; day 1252 teaches it.
Hook avoids superlatives and 'most' claims (claims rule).
Ecclesiastes is presented as an earlier voice saying something similar, not as Ignatius's source.
Editor pass: hook no longer generalizes about what all children, teenagers and adults do; 'Ignatius says' changed to 'the paragraph suggests' for a line he does not write.
